## Basis

This report presents the design of an amine absorber that is to be installed for the treatment of a gas stream. In an amine absorption unit of this kind, the gas is brought into contact with an amine solvent inside a column, and the solvent selectively absorbs the key component from the gas, so that the treated gas leaving the top of the column is substantially freed of that component. The design throughput of the unit is 33 t per day, and the separation duty that the design is required to achieve is the removal of 96% of the key component present in the incoming gas. The materials basis for the design is that all wetted parts, that is, all parts that come into contact with the process fluids, are to be manufactured in 316L stainless steel.

The basis of the design also includes a number of broader assumptions that should be recorded here. The unit is intended for continuous operation, and the design is developed around a steady treating duty rather than around intermittent or batch operation. The solvent circulates between the absorber and its regeneration equipment, and the absorber itself is designed as one part of that circulating system, although the design of the regeneration equipment as such is not the subject of this report. The treated gas specification is expressed in terms of the removal duty stated above, and the design is judged against that duty. Layout, tie-ins, foundations and structures lie outside the scope of the present document.

## Sizing

The sizing of the absorber is governed by two largely separate considerations, namely the diameter of the column and its height, and it is helpful to treat them in turn. The diameter is set by the gas traffic through the column. As the gas rate rises, the gas velocity in the column rises with it, and there is a limiting velocity at which the rising gas begins to hold back the liquid that is trying to flow down, a condition generally known as flooding. The diameter is therefore chosen so that the design gas rate corresponds to a velocity that sits comfortably below the flooding velocity, with a margin that allows the unit to absorb the ordinary fluctuations of operation without approaching the limit. A column that is too narrow will flood and lose its separation; a column that is wider than necessary wastes capital and can, paradoxically, create its own problems of liquid distribution at low rates.

The height of the column is set by the contact that the separation requires. The removal duty is demanding, and the gas and the solvent must be given enough contact, over enough transfer surface, for the key component to pass from the gas into the liquid to the extent that the duty specifies. Height is provided by the internals of the column, which may take the form of trays or of packing, and the choice between these alternatives is one of the main decisions of the design. Trays are robust and tolerant of fouling and of uneven operation, while packing offers a large surface in a given volume and a low pressure drop, at the price of a greater sensitivity to the quality of liquid distribution. In either case, the height must also accommodate the entry and exit arrangements for the gas and the liquid, and the disengagement space in which droplets of solvent are separated from the treated gas before the gas leaves the column.

It is worth adding that the sizing cannot be separated from the solvent circulation, which interacts with both the diameter, through the liquid load, and the height, through the driving force maintained along the column. The design therefore treats circulation, diameter, and height as a single package of decisions.

## Materials

The materials section of the design is concerned mainly with the environment that the wetted parts of the absorber will experience in service, and with whether the specified material is a suitable response to that environment. The environment inside an amine absorber is a demanding one. The solvent is corrosive in its own right, and its corrosiveness increases where it has absorbed the key component and where the temperature is highest. Degradation products form in the solvent over time as it circulates and is regenerated, and some of these products are themselves aggressive towards metals. The result is that the corrosion risk is not uniform over the unit: it concentrates in the regions where the loaded solvent is hottest and where velocities are high enough to strip away protective surface films.

Against that environment, the design specifies a stainless steel grade for the wetted parts, as recorded in the basis. The reasoning is that a stainless grade resists the general corrosive attack of the amine environment far better than an ordinary carbon steel would, and in particular that it avoids the rapid and localised attack that amine systems can inflict on less resistant materials. The specification applies to the column shell where it is wetted, to the internals, and to the wetted parts of the associated nozzles and fittings within the battery limit of this design.

Attention is also given in the design to the details that often decide whether a material specification succeeds in practice. Welds and heat-affected zones are treated as part of the wetted surface, not as exceptions to it. Crevices, in which loaded solvent can stagnate and concentrate, are avoided in the arrangement of the internals wherever the geometry allows. Where dissimilar metals would otherwise meet in the wetted zone, the design keeps them apart or accepts the junction only where the galvanic consequences have been considered. None of these points changes the headline specification, but each of them protects it.

## Risks

Two risks are recorded in this report as open items, and it is important to be clear that neither of them is resolved by the design as it stands. The first is fouling. Fouling is the deposition of material on the internal surfaces of the column, and in an amine unit it can arise from degradation products in the solvent, from contaminants carried in with the feed gas, or from corrosion products generated within the system itself. Its consequences would be felt in the sizing first of all: deposits narrow the passages through the internals, raise the pressure drop, disturb the distribution of liquid, and so erode both the capacity and the separation that the sizing was developed to deliver. The difficulty is that the design cannot presently quantify the risk, because the fouling tendency of the actual feed gas and of the actual solvent over a long campaign is not characterised. Until operating evidence or test evidence exists, fouling remains an open item, and the margins in the sizing should be read with that openness in mind.

The second open item is turndown. The design is developed at the design throughput, but the unit will not always be asked to run at that rate, and its behaviour at reduced rates raises questions that the design point does not answer. At low gas rates the internals may distribute the liquid less evenly, and at low liquid rates parts of the packing or the trays may run partially dry, so that the contact on which the removal duty depends is no longer achieved even though the column is tall enough. The solvent circulation, too, has practical minima below which pumps, level control, and distribution devices cease to behave as the design intends. How far the unit can be turned down while still meeting its removal duty is therefore not established by this report. It is recorded here as an open item, to be settled by the combination of vendor information, operating experience on comparable units, and the detailed design work that follows this report.

## Basis

The unit is an amine absorber treating a gas stream. Gas passes up the column against a down-flowing amine solvent, and the solvent absorbs the key component from the gas, so the treated gas leaves the column substantially freed of that component. Design throughput is 33 t per day. The separation duty is removal of 96% of the key component in the incoming gas. Wetted parts are 316L stainless steel; that specification is stated here once and governs the materials section.

The absorber is one part of a circulating solvent system. Solvent leaves the absorber loaded with the absorbed component, is regenerated elsewhere in the system, and returns lean. Regeneration equipment is outside this report, but the absorber is designed as part of that loop, and its sizing assumes a lean solvent of the quality the loop is intended to deliver. Operation is continuous and the design is developed at a steady treating duty. The treated-gas requirement is the removal duty stated above, and the design stands or falls against it. Layout, tie-ins, foundations and structures are outside the report; its subject is the absorber, the reasoning that fixes its size, and the specification that follows from that reasoning.

## Sizing

Column diameter and column height are set by different limits, and the design treats them separately before combining them.

Diameter is set by gas traffic. Rising gas holds back the down-flowing liquid, and at the flooding velocity the column ceases to separate at all. The diameter is chosen so the design gas rate runs at a velocity held below flooding with a working margin, wide enough to absorb ordinary operating fluctuation and no wider: an oversized column spends capital to no purpose and distributes liquid poorly at low rates, which is the turndown problem recorded in the risks section.

Height is set by the contact the duty requires. The key component must pass from gas to solvent to the extent of the stated removal, and the internals must provide the transfer surface and the contact time that transfer needs. The choice of internals is the main open decision inside the sizing. Trays tolerate fouling and maldistribution and forgive uneven operation. Packing gives more surface per volume and a lower pressure drop, and pays for it with a stricter demand on liquid distribution. Either choice must also accommodate gas and liquid entry arrangements and a disengagement space in which entrained solvent droplets leave the treated gas.

Pressure drop is checked alongside both decisions, because the gas has to be moved through the column at the design rate within the pressure the upstream system can supply, and an internals choice that wins on contact can still fail on pressure drop.

Solvent circulation binds the two decisions together. The circulation rate fixes how much key component each pass of solvent carries, loads the internals with liquid, and maintains the driving force along the column. Diameter, height and circulation are therefore settled as one package. A change to any one of them reopens the other two.

## Materials

The material question is set by the environment the wetted parts meet. Amine solvent is corrosive; loaded solvent, carrying the absorbed component, is more corrosive than lean; and the attack is strongest where the loaded solvent is hottest and where flow strips the protective film from the surface. Degradation products formed in the circulating solvent add to the attack over time. Corrosion risk in this unit is therefore not uniform. It concentrates in defined regions, and the specification answers the concentrated risk, not an average one.

The grade named in the basis is specified for wetted parts on that evidence. A stainless grade resists the general attack of the amine environment and, more importantly, the rapid localised attack that amine systems inflict on plainer materials in exactly the hot, loaded regions identified above. The specification covers the wetted shell, the internals, and the wetted parts of nozzles and fittings within this design's battery limit.

The specification is protected in the details. Welds and heat-affected zones count as wetted surface, with no exception for their different structure. Crevices in which loaded solvent can stagnate and concentrate are avoided in the arrangement of the internals wherever geometry allows. Junctions of dissimilar metals in the wetted zone are kept apart, or accepted only where the galvanic consequence has been examined. The headline specification is one line in the basis; these provisions are what make it hold in the built unit. Inspection access belongs to the same protection: the regions where the risk concentrates are the regions an inspection has to be able to reach, and an arrangement that cannot be inspected cannot be said to be covered by the specification at all.

## Risks

Two risks are open items in this report. Neither is resolved here, and the design is not represented as resolving them.

Fouling is the first. Deposits form on internal surfaces from solvent degradation products, from contaminants entering with the feed gas, and from corrosion products generated inside the system. The consequences land on the sizing: deposits narrow the flow passages, raise pressure drop, and disturb liquid distribution, so capacity and separation both fall away from the values the sizing delivers on clean internals. The risk cannot be quantified in this report. The fouling tendency of the actual feed gas and the actual solvent over a long campaign is uncharacterised, and no test or operating evidence on these streams exists yet. Fouling stays open until such evidence exists, and the sizing margins are to be read as margins against an unquantified risk.

Turndown is the second. The design is developed at the design throughput, and behaviour at reduced rates is not established by designing at that point. At low gas and liquid rates the internals distribute liquid less evenly, packing and tray surfaces can run partially dry, and the contact the removal duty depends on is lost inside a column tall enough to provide it. Solvent circulation has its own practical minima, set by pumping, by level control and by the distribution devices. How far the unit turns down and still meets its removal duty is therefore an open question, to be settled by vendor information, by operating experience on comparable units, and by the detailed design that follows this report.
